faqs.q: How do I convert an hourly rate to an annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work per week, then multiply by 52. For a standard full-time role, we assume 38 hours per week. For example, $30 per hour × 38 hours × 52 weeks = $59,280 per year. If you work fewer or more hours, adjust the weekly figure accordingly. This is gross pay before tax and super.

faqs.q: What is casual loading and how does it affect my pay?
faqs.a: Casual loading is an additional 25% paid on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave (annual leave, sick leave). The Fair Work Ombudsman states that from 1 July 2026, the casual National Minimum Wage is $33.05 per hour, which includes the 25% loading on the base $26.44. When using our calculator, tick the casual loading checkbox to add 25% to your base rate. Do not enter a rate that already includes casual loading.

faqs.q: Is superannuation included in my hourly rate or paid on top?
faqs.a: Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings. The super guarantee rate is 12% of your ordinary time earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year (2026–27). For example, if your annual gross pay is $60,000, your employer must contribute an additional $7,200 into your super fund. This is not deducted from your pay; it is an extra benefit.

## Ally Langdon Nine Network Salary Negotiations: What Your Hourly Rate Really Means

When high-profile roles like those at the Nine Network are negotiated – think of Ally Langdon’s reported salary discussions – the conversation often starts with an annual figure. But understanding the hourly equivalent is crucial, especially if you’re a contractor, casual, or comparing offers across industries. Whether you’re a job seeker or an employer, knowing how to convert an hourly rate to annual pay, factor in casual loading, and account for superannuation can make or break a negotiation.

In this guide, we’ll walk you through the standard conversion formula, explain the difference between the National Minimum Wage and award rates, and show how casual loading and super are paid on top. We’ll also touch on how the Fair Work Ombudsman and Fair Work Commission set the benchmarks that underpin every salary negotiation in Australia.

### The Basic Formula: Hourly to Annual

The simplest way to estimate your annual gross pay is:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

We assume a standard full-time week of 38 hours, as defined by the Fair Work Ombudsman. If you work part-time or casual shifts, replace 38 with your actual weekly hours. For example:

- $30 per hour × 38 hours × 52 weeks = $59,280 per year
- $50 per hour × 38 hours × 52 weeks = $98,800 per year

This gives you the gross amount before tax, Medicare levy, and super. It assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, and no allowances. For a more precise estimate, use our [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) tool or check the [pay guides](/blog) for your award.

### National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates

From 1 July 2026, the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour for employees 21 and over, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. However, most employees are covered by a modern award, which sets higher minimum rates for specific industries and roles. The Fair Work Commission’s Modern Awards Pay Database contains the official rates, allowances, and penalty rates. Award minimum wages increased by 4.75% from 1 July 2026.

If you’re negotiating a salary – like those in the media industry where Ally Langdon works – you should check the relevant award. The Fair Work Ombudsman’s Pay Calculator can help you find the correct minimum rate for your job. Remember, job advertisements cannot offer less than the minimum pay rates and entitlements.

### Casual Loading: 25% on Top

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on their base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave. The casual National Minimum Wage is therefore $33.05 per hour ($26.44 × 1.25). When using our [timesheet](/), you can tick the casual loading checkbox to automatically add 25% to your base rate. **Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading** – let the calculator do the addition.

For example, if your base rate is $30 per hour, the casual rate is $37.50. Over a 38-hour week, that’s $1,425 per week instead of $1,140. That extra $285 per week can significantly affect your annual estimate and your negotiating position.

### Superannuation: Paid on Top

Superannuation is not deducted from your hourly rate; it is an additional contribution your employer must pay into your super fund. From 1 July 2026, the super guarantee rate is 12% of your ordinary time earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. This means if your annual gross pay is $80,000, your employer adds $9,600 to your super account.

When comparing salary offers, always consider the total remuneration package: gross pay plus super. For more details, see our guide on [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging).

### Fortnightly Pay: A Handy Check

Many employers pay fortnightly. To estimate your fortnightly gross pay, simply double your weekly figure. For a full-time worker on the National Minimum Wage:

- Weekly: $1,004.90
- Fortnightly: $2,009.80

This can help you budget and verify your pay slips. The Fair Work Ombudsman requires employers to provide a pay slip for every payment, so you can cross-check.

### Tax and Take-Home Pay

Once you have your annual gross figure, you can estimate your take-home pay using the 2026–27 resident tax rates:

- Nil tax on the first $18,200
- 15% on income between $18,201 and $45,000
- 30% on income between $45,001 and $135,000
- 37% on income between $135,001 and $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus the Medicare levy of 2% (with possible reductions for low-income earners). Our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) tool can do the calculation for you, but note that it does not account for HELP repayments, the Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging.

### Why This Matters in Salary Negotiations

Whether you’re Ally Langdon negotiating a contract with the Nine Network or a graduate starting your first job, understanding the numbers puts you in control. Know your minimum entitlement under the award, factor in casual loading if applicable, and remember that super is an extra cost to the employer. If an employer offers you a salary of $100,000, the true cost to them is at least $112,000 including super. Conversely, if you’re offered an hourly rate, make sure you know whether it includes casual loading.

For more resources, check our [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page and [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) guide. And always keep your own records of hours worked – the Fair Work Ombudsman’s Record my hours app is a free option.

### A Note on Estimates

The calculations on this site are estimates only. They assume a consistent 38-hour week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax uses the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed in this estimate. This is not a determination of your pay or tax. Always consult a qualified professional for personal advice.
